poiANTT-desc:
When the old Antarctic Treaty collapsed in the Dark Age, everyone expected the continent to be carved up. Its ice was retreating, {{poiANTT001|its coasts were opening}}, and the powers that had signed away their claims a century earlier were in no condition to keep their word. It was the people already there who decided otherwise. The crews of the research stations, cut off from governments that no longer answered, pooled their stores, their ships and their sponsors' contracts, and declared the continent held in trust: owned by no nation, licensed to all, and governed by those who live on it.

The Antarctica Trust has kept that arrangement for more than a century. Its land is held in common and leased, never sold. Every mine, field and station on the continent works under a Trust licence, pays into the Trust's fund, and answers to its council at {{poiANTT005|Point Zero}}. It administers Western and Eastern Antarctica, {{poiANTT004|the Transantarctic Zone}} and the new lands the ice has given up, from {{poiANTT003|Mann's Sea}} to {{poiANTT006|the Grand Ice Canyon}}.

The Trust is rich. Beneath the ice lie {{poiANTT002|rare earths and helium}} in quantities found almost nowhere else, along with gas, uranium, iron and coal, and its licences are sought by every bloc on Earth. Conosur is its gateway through Patagonia and Polystralia its supplier across the southern seas. That wealth is also its great contradiction. The Trust was founded to protect a continent, and it pays for itself by digging into it.
poiANTT001-desc:
Greenfield City was founded on the first stretch of coast to thaw for good, and named, with more hope than accuracy, for the moss and lichen that came back with it. Today it is the largest city in Antarctica and its true capital in all but name: a sprawl of insulated housing, greenhouse domes and docks where the supply ships from Patagonia and the Pacific unload.

Its people call themselves Antarcticans, and many of them were born there. They are miners' children and scientists' grandchildren, and they have little patience for foreigners who still talk about the continent as an empty place.
poiANTT002-desc:
The White Lua Mines are the richest workings in Antarctica and the largest single source of the Trust's income. Cut into rock that had not seen daylight for millions of years, they produce rare earths and helium on a scale that the rest of the world, short of both, will pay almost anything for.

The work is brutal. Shafts flood with meltwater, cold kills machinery as surely as it kills people, and the miners who work the deep seams are paid like it. The Trust's licence rules are strictest here, and so are the arguments about them: every new shaft is a vote in the council, and every vote is closer than the last.
poiANTT003-desc: Mann's Sea did not exist a century ago. It opened where a great ice shelf collapsed into the ocean, and it is named after the survey captain who first sailed into it and returned to say it went much further than anyone believed. Its shallow, cold waters hide the Trust's gas fields, and its shores are the newest land on Earth, scraped bare by the ice and still rising as the weight comes off them.
poiANTT004-desc:
The Great Ice Fields are melting, and the water has to go somewhere. Hara's Wall is where the Trust decided it would not go: a barrier of packed ice, rock and concrete that holds back the meltwater lakes above the Transantarctic Zone and releases it in measured channels rather than all at once. It is named after the engineer who designed it and did not live to see it finished.

Every Antarctican knows what lies below it. If the Wall failed, the floods would scour the valleys under the Ice Fields clean, mines and settlements with them. Its maintenance takes a larger share of the Trust's budget each year.
poiANTT005-desc:
Point Zero is the site of the old station at the South Pole, and the only place on the continent that belongs to no licence at all. It is where the Trust's council meets: delegates elected by the settlements and the station crews, sitting with observers sent by the blocs that hold licences, who may speak but not vote.

The arrangement has survived because nobody outside the Trust could agree on anything better. The observers would each prefer a vote of their own, and some would prefer the whole continent. For now they bring proposals, the council listens, and the decisions are made by people who will still be living on the ice when the observers have gone home.
poiANTT006-desc:
In the walls of the Grand Ice Canyon, where the cold is deep and stable, the Trust keeps the vaults. Seeds, tissue samples and genetic records from across the planet are stored there for the Ark Initiative, a library of life held against the day the rest of the world needs to start again.

The Vaults are the reason many Antarcticans give when asked why the Trust exists at all. They are also its most awkward neighbour, sitting a few hours from the mines that pay for them.
